data.title: Mycetoma (Madura foot) — viva
data.summary: Fungal infections · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Mycetoma (Madura foot)** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. Define mycetoma. What is the classic triad?**
- Chronic, progressive, granulomatous, subcutaneous infection caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or aerobic filamentous bacteria (actinomycetoma) after traumatic implantation (thorn prick)
- Triad: painless subcutaneous swelling (tumefaction), multiple sinuses, discharge of grains (granules)

**Q2. Where is the 'mycetoma belt'? Who gets it?**
- Between latitudes ~15° S and 30° N — Sudan, Mexico, India, Senegal, Venezuela
- Barefoot farm workers and herdsmen, young adult males 20–40 years; foot commonest (~70%), then hand, back, scalp, buttocks (carrying sacks/wood)
- In India: Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat; actinomycetoma (Nocardia, Actinomadura) is more frequent in many Indian series, eumycetoma (Madurella) in drier areas

**Q3. Name the causative organisms.**
- Eumycetoma: Madurella mycetomatis (commonest worldwide, black grains), Trematosphaeria grisea, Falciformispora, Scedosporium boydii (white), Acremonium, Fusarium, Exophiala
- Actinomycetoma: Nocardia brasiliensis, N. asteroides, Actinomadura madurae (white/yellow), A. pelletieri (red grains), Streptomyces somaliensis (yellow)

**Q4. What do grain colours tell you?**
- Black grains — always eumycetoma (Madurella, Trematosphaeria, Exophiala)
- Red — Actinomadura pelletieri
- Yellow — Streptomyces somaliensis, Nocardia
- White/pale — Actinomadura madurae, Nocardia, Scedosporium, Acremonium, Fusarium

**Q5. Compare eumycetoma and actinomycetoma.**
- Eumycetoma: slower, well-defined, encapsulated, late bone involvement with few large (>1 cm) punched-out cavities, coarse grains 0.5–2 mm (black/pale), septate hyphae with chlamydospores, treated with azoles + surgery
- Actinomycetoma: faster, ill-defined and inflammatory, early bone involvement with many small cavities ('moth-eaten'), lymph nodes more often, fine grains (20–100 µm) of thin branching Gram-positive filaments (Nocardia acid-fast), responds to antibiotics

**Q6. How do you investigate?**
- Grains from sinus discharge, deep biopsy or FNAC — naked eye colour, KOH mount (eumycetoma: broad septate hyphae), Gram/modified ZN (actinomycetoma: thin filaments)
- Culture: Sabouraud dextrose agar (fungi); brain-heart infusion/LJ (actinomycetes); PCR/sequencing (ITS) for species
- Histopathology: suppurative granulomas around grains (type 1 neutrophils, type 2 macrophage/giant cells, type 3 epithelioid granuloma); Splendore–Hoeppli phenomenon around grains
- Imaging: X-ray (soft-tissue swelling, periosteal reaction, lytic cavities); USG (hyper-reflective grains); MRI 'dot-in-circle' sign — extent before surgery

**Q7. What is the Splendore–Hoeppli phenomenon?**
- Radiating, eosinophilic, club-like material (antigen–antibody complexes) around organisms
- Seen in mycetoma, botryomycosis, sporotrichosis (asteroid bodies), actinomycosis, schistosomiasis, entomophthoromycosis (basidiobolomycosis)

**Q8. What is the dot-in-circle sign?**
- On MRI/USG: small hypointense dot (grain) within hyperintense spheres (granulomatous inflammation) — highly suggestive of mycetoma

**Q9. Treatment of actinomycetoma.**
- Combination antibiotics for months (to prevent resistance)
- Welsh regimen: amikacin 15 mg/kg/day IV + cotrimoxazole (35 mg/kg/day) for 21 days, followed by 15 days of cotrimoxazole alone; repeat 3–4 cycles; cotrimoxazole maintenance afterwards (modified Welsh — add rifampicin 10 mg/kg)
- Two-step regimen (Indian): intensive — penicillin + gentamicin + cotrimoxazole for 5–7 weeks; maintenance — amoxicillin + cotrimoxazole until 2–5 months after cure
- Modified two-step: gentamicin 80 mg IV twice daily + cotrimoxazole DS twice daily for 4 weeks, then cotrimoxazole + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily until 6 months after clinical cure
- Alternatives: dapsone, minocycline, amoxicillin-clavulanate, imipenem, linezolid; monitor renal function and hearing with aminoglycosides

**Q10. Treatment of eumycetoma.**
- Itraconazole 200–400 mg/day (drug of choice) for many months (often 9–12+), combined with surgical debridement/excision of the reduced lesion
- Alternatives: terbinafine 250–1000 mg/day, voriconazole, posaconazole; fosravuconazole under trial
- Amputation for advanced bony disease not responding

**Q11. What are the criteria of cure?**
- Healing of sinuses, disappearance of swelling, normal skin, no grains on FNAC/biopsy, no cavities on USG, return of normal bone on imaging; continue therapy months after clinical cure

**Q12. Differential diagnosis.**
- Botryomycosis (bacterial grains), chronic osteomyelitis, actinomycosis (jaw, sulphur granules, anaerobic Actinomyces israelii), tuberculosis (scrofuloderma, TB of bone), chromoblastomycosis, sporotrichosis, Kaposi sarcoma, soft-tissue tumours, Madura-like cellulitis, filarial lymphoedema

**Q13. How is actinomycosis different from actinomycetoma?**
- Actinomycosis: endogenous anaerobic Actinomyces israelii (commensal of mouth/gut), cervicofacial ('lumpy jaw'), thoracic, abdominal; sulphur granules; treat with long penicillin
- Actinomycetoma: exogenous aerobic actinomycetes (Nocardia, Actinomadura, Streptomyces), implantation on foot

**Q14. Complications and prognosis?**
- Bone destruction, deformity, disability, secondary bacterial infection, lymphatic spread, rarely visceral spread (back mycetoma → spine, lung)
- Actinomycetoma — good cure rates with combination therapy; eumycetoma — high relapse, often surgery/amputation needed

**Q15. Classify subcutaneous mycoses (PYQ short note).**
- Mycetoma, sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis, phaeohyphomycosis, entomophthoromycosis (basidiobolomycosis, conidiobolomycosis), rhinosporidiosis (now Mesomycetozoea), lobomycosis, subcutaneous zygomycosis

**Q16. What is phaeohyphomycosis?**
- Infection by dematiaceous (brown-black) fungi that appear as pigmented septate hyphae/yeast-like cells in tissue (no muriform cells, no grains) — subcutaneous cysts (Exophiala), sinus, cerebral forms; treat with excision + itraconazole

## Quick spotter facts
- Swelling + sinuses + grains — mycetoma
- Black grains = always fungal
- Dot-in-circle sign on MRI

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 19A (Subcutaneous mycoses — mycetoma, Tables 19A.8–19A.10). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
